description: Giving components a memory with the useState hook.

screens.body:
A normal variable inside a component resets every time the component re-renders — amnesia by default. State is the fix: a value React remembers between renders.

Click a like button and the count must survive. Typing in a search box, toggling dark mode, opening a menu — all state.

options: To make the page load faster
check.question: Why do components need state?

screens.heading: State is a component's memory

screens.body:
const [count, setCount] = useState(0) gives you two things in one line: the current value, and a setter function that updates it.

The argument — 0 here — is the initial value, used only the very first time. The names are yours to choose, but the value-then-setter pattern is always the same.

options: A pair: the current value and a setter function
check.question: What does useState return?

screens.heading: useState gives you a pair

screens.body:
Calling setCount(5) does two things: it stores the new value, then it tells React to re-render the component so the screen shows it.

You never touch the screen directly. Update the state, and React repaints. That's the whole deal — state in, UI out.

options: React stores the value and re-renders the component
The value changes but the screen stays the same
check.question: What happens when you call a state setter?

screens.heading: The setter re-renders the screen
screens.keyPoint: Set state → React re-renders. You never touch the DOM.

screens.body:
useState(0) uses 0 only on the very first render. On every render after that, React ignores the argument and hands you the remembered value.

So re-renders never reset your state back to the initial value — that's exactly why it's a memory and not just a variable.

options: Only when the setter is called
check.question: When is the useState argument used?

screens.heading: The initial value runs once

screens.body:
Render two <Counter /> components on one page and each keeps its own independent count. Clicking one never affects the other.

State lives with the component instance, not with the code. Same recipe, separate memories.

options: Only that one updates; each has its own state
check.question: Two <Counter /> components on a page — what happens when you click one?

screens.heading: Each component gets its own state
screens.keyPoint: Same component code, separate state per instance.

screens.body:
To add one, write setCount(count + 1). When several updates happen fast, use the updater form: setCount(c => c + 1) — React hands you the latest value.

The updater form is the safe choice inside timers, loops, or rapid clicks where count might be stale.

check.question: What's the safe way to add 1 when updates may pile up?

screens.heading: Update from the old value
screens.keyPoint: setCount(c => c + 1) always uses the freshest value.

screens.body:
Writing count = count + 1 or pushing into a state array changes the value behind React's back — no re-render happens and the screen goes stale.

Always go through the setter. The setter is the only door React watches.

options: React won't know, so it won't re-render
check.question: Why can't you write count = count + 1 directly?

screens.heading: Never mutate state directly
screens.keyPoint: The setter is the only way to update state.
